agenda: Reports of the Secretary-General on the Sudan and South Sudan
members: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland

steps.intent: The United States aims to de-escalate cross-border spillover between Sudan and South Sudan, condemn attacks by the RSF and SAF, stop reported drone and weapons transfers through South Sudanese territory, restore the Greater Nile Oil Pipeline, and reinforce humanitarian access and accountability. The most difficult point is Russia, which previously vetoed a broader Sudan ceasefire text; to avoid a veto, the draft avoids new sanctions and an explicit Chapter VII enforcement posture while still pressing both parties. China and some elected members may seek to soften the language on South Sudan’s role, so the balance between condemning external support and respecting South Sudanese sovereignty will be key to reaching at least nine votes.

messages.Algeria: Algeria supports a balanced text that addresses the conflict in the Sudan and its spillover into South Sudan. We ask the penholder to ensure OP1 affirms a Sudanese-owned and Sudanese-led political process and full respect for Sudan's sovereignty, and to revise OP4 so that reports of transfers are verified and all regional States are called upon without singling out South Sudan. We also seek a positive reference to the Sudanese Government's facilitation of humanitarian access and a safeguard that arms embargoes do not impede implementation of the Revitalized Agreement.
messages.China: China supports a balanced text that presses for ceasefire, humanitarian access and peaceful resolution of Sudan-South Sudan issues. However, we have serious concerns with OP4's direct condemnation of South Sudan and OP6's new reporting task for the Panel of Experts, which risk prejudging facts and imposing excessive pressure. We ask the penholder to reflect these changes so that the Council speaks with one voice while respecting sovereignty and regional ownership.
messages.Denmark: Denmark welcomes the US draft and supports its core objectives of ceasefire, humanitarian access, accountability and respect for sovereignty. We ask the penholder to correct or qualify the unverified reference to an MSF hospital, strengthen language on inclusive political participation and accountability for sexual and gender-based violence, and signal readiness to consider further arms measures if arms flows continue. Denmark can support the text with these targeted amendments.
messages.France: France welcomes the penholder’s draft and supports its core objectives, particularly on humanitarian access, protection of civilians and cross-border arms flows. We ask for a clearer demand for a sustained ceasefire, stronger language on conflict-related sexual violence and grave violations against children, and legal precision on arms transfers and accountability. We also believe the text should expressly support the Secretary-General’s Personal Envoy for the Sudan and include the International Criminal Court in the accountability framework.
messages.Greece: Greece thanks the United States for the balanced draft and supports its overall direction. We ask for targeted additions on the March 2025 attack against UN personnel in Nasir County, on medical neutrality and accountability, and on the regional refugee and returnee impact of the Sudan crisis. We also suggest regular follow-up reporting so the Council can track cross-border and humanitarian developments. Greece remains ready to work with the penholder and all members to strengthen consensus.
messages.Guyana: Guyana supports the draft’s core objectives and thanks the United States for its penholdership. We ask that OP1 clearly reflect an inclusive, Sudanese-led and Sudanese-owned political process and that PP5 and OP4 explicitly address foreign interference. We also seek language in OP5 urging Sudan to reconsider the pipeline shutdown and avoid measures that worsen the humanitarian and economic situation in South Sudan, and in OP6 confirming that the Panel of Experts acts within its existing mandate under resolution 1591 (2005). These changes would strengthen African ownership and Council unity.
messages.Pakistan: Pakistan supports the Council's objective of de-escalation, humanitarian access and respect for the sovereignty of Sudan and South Sudan. However, we cannot support language that expands UNMISS reporting beyond its mandate or politicizes peacekeeping; OP9 must be brought clearly within UNMISS's mandate and host-state coordination. We also seek balanced, verification-based language on cross-border allegations in OP4, rather than attributing responsibility to South Sudan on the basis of reports, and minor adjustments to OP6 to keep the Panel's reporting within its existing mandate.
messages.Panama: Panama supports the draft's focus on civilian protection, humanitarian access and accountability and can support it with targeted adjustments. We ask that the transition language be clearly Sudanese-led and inclusive; that conflict-related sexual and gender-based violence be explicitly condemned; and that climate-related humanitarian risk language consistent with resolution 2779 be included. We also seek clearer reference to refugees and returnees and independent verification of the reported arms transfers under OP4.
messages.Republic of Korea: The Republic of Korea supports the draft’s focus on cessation of hostilities, civilian protection and cross-border spillover. As Chair of the 1591 Sanctions Committee, we would strongly prefer OP6 to explicitly recall the Sudan arms embargo and the Committee’s reporting role. We also seek reinforced humanitarian access language, including the Adré corridor, and a reference to conflict-related sexual violence and grave violations against children.
messages.Russian Federation: We support the humanitarian and ceasefire thrust of the text and the call to resolve the pipeline issue through dialogue. However, we cannot accept unverified accusations against South Sudan or the expansion of the Panel of Experts' role, which is inconsistent with its mandate. We request neutral language on weapons transfers and national ownership of accountability; otherwise we will be unable to support the draft.
messages.Sierra Leone: Sierra Leone supports the thrust of the draft and thanks the United States for its consultations. We seek factual precision on incidents, a balanced formulation on reported cross-border transfers that respects South Sudan's sovereignty and calls for investigation rather than prejudging, and explicit protection language for women and children. We also ask that reporting remain evidence-based and consistent with UNMISS's existing mandate and host-state cooperation.
messages.Slovenia: Slovenia supports the draft's clear condemnation of the RSF shelling and its focus on cross-border military support and humanitarian access. We would like the text to reflect more explicitly the grave violations against women and children and ethnically motivated violence, and to strengthen accountability language, including that violations may amount to international crimes. We also suggest reinforcing sustained humanitarian access to Darfur and other conflict-affected areas and women's meaningful participation in peace processes.
messages.Somalia: Somalia thanks the United States for the draft and supports its core objectives. We ask the penholder to anchor the text more firmly in African-led mediation and respect for the sovereignty of Sudan and South Sudan, and to balance the Sudan-focused provisions with clear support for the Revitalized Agreement. We also recommend that reports of cross-border transfers be subject to Panel of Experts verification while still requiring full compliance with sanctions and arms embargoes.
messages.United Kingdom of Great Britain and Nort: The United Kingdom supports the thrust of the United States draft and welcomes its focus on RSF attacks, cross-border support and humanitarian access. We ask the penholder to strengthen OP9 with explicit language on UNMISS freedom of movement and non-interference, and to sharpen OP4 into a demand on South Sudan and all Member States to halt such transfers. We also want OP8 to name conflict-related sexual violence and child recruitment, and to correct the unverified hospital reference in OP2. We are ready to work constructively.

replies.Algeria: partially accepted: OP1, Adré language and OP6 safeguards included; OP4 recast around verification and all Member States rather than a specific regional call.
replies.China: partially accepted: OP4 neutralized, OP6 avoids a new Panel task and uses existing reporting channels, and OP9 is tied to UNMISS's mandate and consultation.
replies.Denmark: partially accepted: MSF reference qualified as reported, OP1 participation strengthened, and OP8 includes sexual and gender-based violence and children; further arms-measure language not included.
replies.France: partially accepted: OP1 sustained ceasefire, SGBV/children language, and the Secretary-General's Personal Envoy included; ICC reference omitted.
replies.Greece: accepted: Nasir attack, refugee/returnee impact and periodic reporting every ninety days included.
replies.Guyana: partially accepted: OP1 Sudanese-led transition and pipeline reconsideration included; Panel language removed to avoid a new mandate task.
replies.Pakistan: accepted: OP9 brought within UNMISS's mandate and host-state coordination, and OP4/OP6 use verification and existing channels.
replies.Panama: accepted: OP1, SGBV, climate language, refugees/returnees and verification through appropriate UN mechanisms included.
replies.Republic of Korea: partially accepted: 1591 Committee reporting and SGBV/children language included; explicit embargo citations limited to applicable measures.
replies.Russian Federation: partially accepted: named accusations and Panel reporting tasks removed and OP4/PP6 neutralized; accountability language retained in general form.
replies.Sierra Leone: partially accepted: verification and explicit SGBV/child protection included; MSF retained as a reported incident rather than deleted.
replies.Slovenia: accepted: SGBV, ethnically motivated violence, international crimes, sustained access to Darfur and Kordofan, and women's participation included.
replies.Somalia: partially accepted: OP1 AU/IGAD language, OP5 good offices and new R-ARCSS implementation paragraph included; OP4 does not task the Panel specifically.
replies.United Kingdom of Great Britain and Nort: partially accepted: OP9 freedom of movement and non-interference strengthened and SGBV/children language added; OP4 softened to preserve P5 consensus.

steps.summary: The revised draft preserves the core US objectives on ceasefire, humanitarian access, accountability and South Sudan's peace process while neutralizing the most veto-sensitive language on weapons transfers and Panel of Experts tasks. It is expected to attract broad support without a negative P5 vote.

Insert after 'parties to the conflict in the Sudan': 'including reports that the Government of South Sudan has facilitated transfers of unmanned aerial systems to the Rapid Support Forces'; and insert after 'arms embargoes': 'and demands that the Government of South Sudan immediately cease any such support and exercise effective control over its territory'.

Delete 'the reported attack on 3 May 2025 against a Médecins Sans Frontières hospital,' unless it is substantiated in the Secretary-General's reporting, and replace it with 'the reported destruction at Nyala Airport on 3 May 2025 of an aircraft carrying drones destined for the RSF'.

messages.Algeria: Algeria supports the revised text. We appreciate the inclusion of our key safeguards on Sudanese sovereignty, the Adré crossing, and the implementation of arms embargoes without impeding the Revitalized Agreement. The recast OP4, with its focus on verification through existing United Nations mechanisms and its call on all Member States, addresses our concerns, and we are ready to vote in favour.
messages.China: China thanks the penholder for the revised text and notes that our core concerns on sovereignty, non-interference, existing reporting channels and consultation with host Governments have been reflected. China supports the current draft and will vote in favour. We encourage the Council to remain united and to respect Sudanese and South Sudanese ownership and the principle of African solutions to African problems.
messages.Denmark: Denmark supports the revised draft and welcomes the strengthened language on civilian transition, accountability and conflict-related sexual and gender-based violence. We continue to believe OP6 should signal that the Council will consider further measures, including a comprehensive arms embargo on the Sudan, if violations and arms flows persist. This is important for the Council's credibility and deterrence; with that addition, Denmark is prepared to support the resolution.
messages.France: France welcomes the revised draft and particularly the sustained ceasefire, SGBV and children language, and the inclusion of the Secretary-General’s Personal Envoy. We continue to believe that OP4 should be anchored explicitly in violations of applicable resolutions and arms embargoes, so that it does not create ambiguity for legitimate bilateral cooperation. On accountability, France regrets that the ICC reference was omitted and asks the penholder to restore it, in line with resolution 1593 (2005); this is important for France.
messages.Greece: Greece welcomes the penholder’s incorporation of our earlier requests on the Nasir attack, refugee and returnee impact, and periodic reporting. The text is balanced and reflects our priorities on sovereignty, humanitarian access, accountability and the protection of civilians. We support the draft as it stands and encourage the Council to move to a vote.
messages.Guyana: Guyana supports the revised text and appreciates the incorporation of language on a Sudanese-led civilian transition and reconsideration of the Greater Nile Oil Pipeline shutdown. To strengthen the Council’s response, we ask that PP6 expressly capture foreign interference among the arms-transfer concerns and that OP4 name the Panel of Experts on the Sudan, within its existing mandate under resolution 1591, as an appropriate existing mechanism. These changes are important for A3+ coherence and do not create a new mandate.
messages.Pakistan: Pakistan thanks the penholder for accepting key improvements on OP9, OP4 and OP6. However, OP9 still retains "military" reporting, which goes beyond UNMISS's mandate and the host-state coordination we insisted on; this must be deleted. We also seek OP6 and OP13 to be anchored in existing mandates and reporting channels and to require consultation with the Governments of the Sudan and South Sudan. With these adjustments, Pakistan can support the text.
messages.Panama: Panama supports the revised draft and appreciates the inclusion of our earlier language on a Sudanese-led and inclusive civilian transition, conflict-related sexual and gender-based violence, climate risk, refugees and returnees, and verification through UN mechanisms. We ask the penholder to add an explicit call for all States and parties to cooperate fully with that verification. With this adjustment, Panama is ready to support the text.
messages.Republic of Korea: The Republic of Korea supports the revised draft and welcomes the incorporation of 1591 Committee reporting, strengthened humanitarian access language, and provisions on conflict-related sexual and gender-based violence and children. We appreciate the penholder’s efforts to accommodate our priorities and can join consensus on the text. We encourage all Council members to support the draft and call for its full implementation once adopted.
messages.Russian Federation: We appreciate that the penholder has removed the named accusations and Panel reporting tasks and has neutralized PP6 and OP4. We can support the text if the remaining references to cross-border military reporting are removed and the pipeline paragraph does not single out the Government of the Sudan. Our minor amendment to OP1 should also be reflected.
messages.Sierra Leone: Sierra Leone thanks the United States for incorporating verification and explicit language on conflict-related sexual violence and children, and we accept the MSF reference as a reported incident. We can support the draft with two remaining changes: OP4 should specify transparent and impartial verification with cooperation from all parties, including South Sudan, and OP9 should include reporting on progress toward the gradual relocation of the Tomping base, consistent with the A3+ position. We are ready to join consensus if these refinements are reflected.
messages.Slovenia: Slovenia supports the revised text and welcomes the incorporation of our earlier proposals on conflict-related sexual violence, ethnically motivated violence, accountability for international crimes, sustained humanitarian access to Darfur and Kordofan, and women's participation. We ask for two final refinements: OP8 should explicitly name the Panel of Experts on the Sudan and the Commission on Human Rights in South Sudan, and OP9 should not condition UN reporting on coordination or consultation with host Governments, which risks undermining impartial reporting. With these changes, Slovenia is ready to support the resolution.
messages.Somalia: Somalia supports the revised text and welcomes the inclusion of AU/IGAD language, good offices and the R-ARCSS implementation paragraph. One remaining important point is OP4: the Council should condemn transfers fueling the conflict and explicitly task the Panel of Experts on the Sudan, within its existing mandate, to verify these reports. This strengthens credibility without creating new mechanisms, and Somalia can support the text with this adjustment.
messages.United Kingdom of Great Britain and Nort: The United Kingdom supports the draft and thanks the United States for its work. We need OP9 to preserve independent UN reporting by removing the host-government consultation language. We continue to press for OP4 to name and demand an end to South Sudan's reported facilitation of UAV transfers to the RSF, and we ask that the unsubstantiated MSF hospital reference in OP2 be removed unless verified.

replies.Denmark: rejected: no new arms-embargo readiness language, to preserve Council consensus and avoid new measures
replies.France: partially accepted: OP4 violations language accepted; ICC reference not included
replies.Guyana: rejected: foreign-interference and Panel-of-Experts additions omitted to preserve balance
replies.Pakistan: accepted: OP9 military reporting removed and OP6/OP13 anchored with consultation
replies.Russian Federation: partially accepted: military reporting removed and pipeline balanced; OP1 retains civilian-led transition with agreed-by-Sudanese wording
replies.Sierra Leone: accepted: transparent/impartial verification, South Sudan cooperation, and Tomping reporting included
replies.Slovenia: partially accepted: consultation removed and no-interference stressed; OP8 naming and national-ownership deletion not included
replies.Somalia: rejected: OP4 condemnation and Panel naming not included; balanced verification language retained
replies.United Kingdom: partially accepted: OP9 host-government consultation deleted; South Sudan-specific UAV language and OP2 change not included

steps.summary: The revision incorporates the P5 red lines on OP9 consultation and Russian/Pakistani concerns on military reporting and pipeline balance, while retaining a neutral verification and accountability text. It accepts several A3+ and non-permanent requests but leaves out controversial arms-embargo, ICC, Panel-naming and South Sudan-specific UAV language to protect consensus. The draft is expected to attract 10 yes votes with 5 abstentions and no negative votes.

reasons.Algeria: Algeria had already signalled support and the draft aligns with its priorities: ceasefire, humanitarian access, sovereignty, African-led mediation, and no new punitive measures. It will vote yes.
reasons.China: China’s last negotiation position was support, and the draft retains balanced language on sovereignty, humanitarian access, and African-led mediation without imposing new sanctions or excessive pressure. No red line warrants abstention or veto.
reasons.Denmark: Denmark voted in favour because the resolution advances ceasefire, humanitarian access and accountability aims and preserves Council consensus, despite its important but rejected request on arms-embargo readiness being explained publicly. Blocking or abstaining would be disproportionate given the overall alignment with Denmark’s priorities.
reasons.France: France supports the draft’s core priorities on ceasefire, humanitarian access, sovereignty and accountability, and the OP4 language was partially accepted. Although the ICC reference was omitted, that is not a reason for France to oppose or veto a balanced US penholder text.
reasons.Greece: Greece supported the previous Sudan/South Sudan resolutions and the draft aligns with its positions on international law, humanitarian access, civilian protection, sovereignty, and African-led diplomacy. No Greek red lines were rejected in the last negotiation round.
reasons.Guyana: Guyana has consistently supported Council action on Sudan and South Sudan and has voted in favour of similar texts despite unmet amendments, while using explanations of vote to flag concerns. It will support this draft while reiterating its concerns on foreign interference and the 1591 Panel of Experts.
reasons.Pakistan: Pakistan’s key requested changes to OP6, OP9 and OP13 were accepted, and the draft aligns with Pakistan’s support for sovereignty, humanitarian access, African-led mediation and ceasefire efforts. Therefore Pakistan should vote in favour.
reasons.Panama: Panama has consistently supported Council action on Sudan and South Sudan and its key request on OP4 was accepted, so it would vote in favour while emphasizing humanitarian access, sovereignty, accountability and regional mediation.
reasons.Republic of Korea: The Republic of Korea has consistently supported Security Council action on Sudan and South Sudan, voted in favour of all recent related resolutions, and had no outstanding requests in the final negotiation round. It would therefore support the US draft without needing a pre-vote explanation.
reasons.Russian Federation: Russia's key requested changes on military reporting, balanced pipeline language, and sovereignty were largely accommodated, so it would support rather than abstain. It would still state reservations on externally prescribed transition language and unverified arms-transfer allegations.
reasons.Sierra Leone: Sierra Leone supported the draft with changes, and the penholder accepted its key OP4 verification/cooperation language and OP9 Tomping reporting request; in line with its record and priorities, it should vote in favour.
reasons.Slovenia: Slovenia has consistently voted in favour of Security Council texts on the Sudan/South Sudan crisis, especially those addressing humanitarian access, civilian protection and accountability. The draft aligns with its priorities and its requested changes were at least partially accommodated, so abstention or opposition would not fit its established record.
reasons.Somalia: Somalia’s priorities—ceasefire, humanitarian access, sovereignty, and AU/IGAD mediation—are reflected in the draft, and opposing it over the rejected OP4 change would undermine broader African peace efforts. Somalia therefore votes in favour while continuing to stress robust verification of arms transfers.
reasons.United Kingdom of Great Britain and Nort: The UK consistently supports Council action on humanitarian access, civilian protection and UNMISS in Sudan and South Sudan, and the draft broadly aligns with those priorities despite unmet drafting concerns. It would vote in favour while using its explanation to flag independent reporting and external arms transfers.
reasons.United States of America: The draft is U.S.-submitted and closely reflects long-standing U.S. priorities on Sudan/South Sudan: humanitarian access, civilian protection, accountability, and preventing regional spillover. The United States would strongly support adoption and explain its vote before the vote.

before.Algeria: Algeria will vote in favour of this draft resolution. We do so because it responds to the urgent need to protect civilians, demand a cessation of hostilities, and facilitate safe and unhindered humanitarian access in the Sudan, while addressing the spillover effects on South Sudan and the wider region. We welcome the text’s reaffirmation of the sovereignty, independence, territorial integrity and national unity of the Sudan and South Sudan, and its respect for the principle of African solutions to African problems, including the central roles of the African Union and IGAD. We also note that the draft does not impose new sanctions; it calls for verification through existing mechanisms and for compliance with applicable measures. Algeria stresses that all parties must protect civilians and civilian infrastructure, that humanitarian access must not be obstructed, and that outstanding bilateral issues, including the Greater Nile Oil Pipeline, should be resolved through dialogue. We support this balanced text and call for its full and faithful implementation.
before.Denmark: Denmark thanks the United States for its efforts to keep the Council focused on the devastating conflict in Sudan and its impact on South Sudan and the wider region. We remain deeply alarmed by the continued violence, including the RSF shelling of Abu Shouk camp, attacks on humanitarian and medical personnel, and persistent obstruction of humanitarian access. Denmark will vote in favour of this resolution because it sends an important message on cessation of hostilities, protection of civilians, unhindered humanitarian access, accountability and the need for a Sudanese-led civilian transition. We regret, however, that our proposal in OP6 — to signal the Council’s readiness to consider further measures, including a comprehensive arms embargo, should violations and arms flows continue — was not retained. Denmark believes such a signal is needed to deter further arms transfers and escalation. We also stress the importance of full implementation of the Revitalized Agreement and the full, equal, safe and meaningful participation of women in all peace and political processes. While the text could have gone further, we support it as a constructive step and will continue to advocate for stronger action.
before.France: France votes in favour of the draft resolution. The text responds to the urgency of the crisis in Sudan and South Sudan: it demands a ceasefire, safe and unhindered humanitarian access, respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity, and accountability for serious violations. France regrets that its request for an express reference to the International Criminal Court and resolution 1593 (2005) concerning Darfur was not included. Accountability remains indispensable, and we call on all parties to cooperate with the ICC. France nevertheless supports this balanced text and urges its full implementation.
before.Greece: Mr. President, Greece will vote in favour of the draft resolution. We support its balanced focus on an immediate cessation of hostilities, protection of civilians, safe and unhindered humanitarian access, accountability, and full respect for the sovereignty, independence, territorial integrity and national unity of the Sudan and South Sudan. Greece strongly condemns attacks against civilians, humanitarian personnel and civilian infrastructure, including the shelling of Abu Shouk camp, and calls on all parties to de-escalate, resolve bilateral issues including the Greater Nile Oil Pipeline through dialogue, cooperate with UNMISS, and work with the African Union and IGAD towards an inclusive, Sudanese-led political transition.
before.Guyana: Guyana thanks the United States for its efforts and will vote in favour of this draft resolution. We do so because it demands a ceasefire, safe and unhindered humanitarian access, protection of civilians, respect for the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Sudan and South Sudan, and accountability for serious violations. We remain concerned, however, that the text does not adequately reflect the risks posed by foreign interference and the importance of the Panel of Experts established pursuant to resolution 1591 (2005) in verifying reports of arms transfers. We regret that our proposed additions were not retained. Nonetheless, Guyana supports this draft as a necessary and urgent Council response and urges its full implementation.
before.Pakistan: Pakistan will vote in favour of the draft resolution. We appreciate that some of our concerns were accommodated, including the removal of cross-border military reporting and anchoring requests to the Secretary-General in existing mandates and in consultation with the Governments of the Sudan and South Sudan. At the same time, we reiterate that the mandates of United Nations peacekeeping missions should not be politicized and should be tailored to needs on the ground. We support the draft’s call for a ceasefire, safe and unhindered humanitarian access, respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity, and an inclusive Sudanese-led process with African ownership. We call on all parties to cooperate in good faith and on the Council to maintain a unified voice in support of peace.
before.Panama: Panama votes in favour of this draft resolution. We welcome the inclusion of our requested language in operative paragraph 4 calling upon all Member States and parties to cooperate fully with verification through appropriate United Nations mechanisms. Panama strongly supports the demands for an immediate cessation of hostilities, safe and unhindered humanitarian access, protection of civilians and humanitarian personnel, and full respect for the sovereignty, territorial integrity and national unity of the Sudan and South Sudan. We underscore the need for accountability, the full and meaningful participation of women, and peaceful resolution of bilateral issues, including through regional mediation led by the African Union and IGAD. We call on all parties to comply with their obligations and to engage in good faith towards an inclusive, Sudanese-led political transition.
before.Russian Federation: The Russian Federation will support this draft. We note that a number of our substantive concerns were taken into account: the text no longer introduces new military monitoring tasks and instead places reporting firmly within existing mandates and in consultation with the host Governments; and it adopts a more balanced approach to the Greater Nile Oil Pipeline, calling on both Governments to resolve their bilateral issues through dialogue. We also welcome the emphasis on the sovereignty, territorial integrity and national unity of the Sudan and South Sudan, and on African-led mediation. At the same time, we wish to make clear our understanding that references to a political transition must not be interpreted as an external prescription. The process must remain genuinely Sudanese-led and Sudanese-owned, with its parameters agreed by the Sudanese people, including a transition if they so decide. Any discussion of alleged arms transfers must be handled through verified, impartial and transparent existing mechanisms, without eroding the sovereignty of States or creating new monitoring structures. On this basis, the Russian Federation votes in favour.
before.Sierra Leone: Sierra Leone votes in favour of this draft resolution. We thank the penholder for the constructive engagement and for incorporating key concerns, including transparent and impartial verification of reports of arms transfers and cooperation by all parties, including the Government of South Sudan, as well as reporting on cooperation between UNMISS and the Government of South Sudan, including the gradual relocation of the Tomping base. Sierra Leone remains deeply concerned by the humanitarian and security situation in the Sudan and South Sudan, including attacks on civilians, humanitarian personnel and medical facilities. We support the resolution’s emphasis on cessation of hostilities, safe and unhindered humanitarian access, accountability, respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity, and the full implementation of the Revitalized Agreement. Sierra Leone will continue to work with the Council and regional partners to advance peace, civilian protection and the peaceful resolution of outstanding bilateral issues.
before.Slovenia: Slovenia will vote in favour of this draft resolution. We thank the United States for its efforts to bridge positions. The situation in the Sudan and its spillover into South Sudan demand a clear and unified Council response: an immediate cessation of hostilities, safe and unhindered humanitarian access, protection of civilians, including women and children, and accountability for violations of international humanitarian law and human rights law. We welcome the strengthened language on UNMISS operating without political interference, and we regret that other proposals on accountability were not fully reflected; nonetheless, we support this text as a basis for action. We call on all parties to implement it in full, in respect for the sovereignty, independence, territorial integrity and national unity of the Sudan and South Sudan, with the support of the African Union and IGAD.
before.Somalia: Thank you, President. Somalia will vote in favour of this draft. We support its central demands for an immediate cessation of hostilities, sustained humanitarian access, protection of civilians and civilian infrastructure, and full respect for the sovereignty, territorial integrity, independence and national unity of the Sudan and South Sudan. Somalia welcomes the emphasis on African-led mediation through the African Union and IGAD. We continue to believe that reports of weapons and military materiel transfers must be addressed seriously and verified transparently through existing United Nations mechanisms, including the Panel of Experts on the Sudan within its mandate. We call on all Member States and parties to comply with applicable sanctions and arms embargoes, cooperate with verification, and resolve bilateral issues, including the Greater Nile Oil Pipeline, peacefully and through dialogue.
before.United Kingdom of Great Britain and Nort: The United Kingdom thanks the United States for its efforts to bring the Council together on the grave situation in Sudan and South Sudan. We condemn in the strongest terms the RSF shelling of Abu Shouk camp, attacks on civilians and humanitarian and medical personnel, and all violations of international humanitarian law. We are gravely concerned by reports of arms and unmanned aerial systems transfers to the parties, including reports concerning South Sudan, and we call on all States and parties to respect applicable arms embargoes and to cease any support that fuels the conflict. We also stress that United Nations reporting, including UNMISS reporting, must remain independent and not subject to political interference, and that humanitarian access must be safe, rapid and unhindered. While the text could have gone further in some areas, the United Kingdom will vote in favour of this resolution and urges all parties to implement it without delay.
before.United States of America: Thank you, Mr. President. The United States will vote in favour of this draft resolution, which we have submitted because the Security Council cannot remain silent while Sudan faces the world’s largest humanitarian crisis and while the conflict risks spilling further into South Sudan and the wider region. The RSF’s shelling of Abu Shouk camp and attacks on medical facilities are unconscionable, and all parties, including the SAF and the RSF, must cease hostilities, protect civilians, and allow safe and unhindered humanitarian access. This text also rightly addresses the destabilizing flow of arms and military materiel, the economic and humanitarian impact of the Greater Nile Oil Pipeline shutdown, and the need for accountability and a Sudanese-led, civilian-led political transition in full respect for Sudan’s sovereignty and territorial integrity. We urge all Council members to support the resolution and all parties to implement it in good faith.

after.China:
Mr. President,

China voted in favour of the draft resolution just adopted. We welcome the Council’s unified action at a time when the humanitarian situation in the Sudan and South Sudan is grave and the risk of spillover is increasing. China supports the resolution’s call for an immediate cessation of hostilities, protection of civilians, safe and unhindered humanitarian access and accountability for serious violations.

China has consistently held that the sovereignty, independence, territorial integrity and national unity of the Sudan and South Sudan must be fully respected. The future of the two countries should be decided by their own people. The international community should support, not impose, a Sudanese-led and Sudanese-owned political process and African-led mediation through the African Union and IGAD. We welcome the resolution’s reaffirmation of these principles.

We call on all parties to cease hostilities, protect civilians and civilian infrastructure, including medical and humanitarian personnel, and facilitate humanitarian access. The shutdown of the Greater Nile Oil Pipeline should be resolved through dialogue and consultation. As a major troop-contributing country to UNMISS, China will continue to support the Mission in implementing its mandate in line with the needs of the host country.

On reports of arms transfers, verification should be conducted through existing United Nations mechanisms, in a transparent and impartial manner, with respect for sovereignty and in consultation with host Governments. We welcome that the resolution does not introduce new sanctions or new monitoring mechanisms. Humanitarian issues should not be politicized. China will continue to play a constructive role in promoting peace and development in the Sudan and South Sudan.

Thank you, Mr. President.
after.Republic of Korea: Thank you, Mr. President. The Republic of Korea voted in favour of this resolution and welcomes its adoption. We remain gravely concerned by the continued hostilities in the Sudan, including the RSF shelling of Abu Shouk camp and attacks against medical and humanitarian personnel, and by the risk of spillover into South Sudan and the wider region. The Council has sent a clear message: all parties must cease hostilities, agree to a sustained ceasefire, protect civilians, and ensure safe and unhindered humanitarian access. We call on all Member States and parties to respect the sovereignty, territorial integrity and national unity of the Sudan and South Sudan, to comply fully with applicable sanctions and arms embargoes, and to cooperate with transparent and impartial verification through existing United Nations mechanisms, including the Panel of Experts within its mandate. We also urge the Governments of the Sudan and South Sudan to resolve bilateral issues, including the Greater Nile Oil Pipeline, through dialogue. Accountability for serious violations must be pursued, and the full, equal, safe and meaningful participation of women must be ensured. The Republic of Korea will continue to support the Council’s unified efforts and African-led mediation, including by the African Union and IGAD.
after.United States of America: Thank you, Mr. President. The United States welcomes the unanimous adoption of this resolution and thanks Council members for their constructive engagement. The Security Council has spoken with one voice at a moment when the people of Sudan and South Sudan urgently need it to. This resolution is not an end in itself; it is a clear demand for immediate de-escalation, safe and unhindered humanitarian access, protection of civilians and civilian infrastructure, accountability for serious violations, and a genuine Sudanese-led, civilian-led political transition. The United States calls on the SAF and RSF to cease hostilities without delay, agree to a sustained ceasefire, and engage in good faith. We call on all Member States and parties to respect applicable arms embargoes, cease transfers that fuel the conflict, and cooperate fully with transparent and impartial verification through existing United Nations mechanisms. The shutdown of the Greater Nile Oil Pipeline underscores the need for dialogue on bilateral issues that affect the stability and livelihoods of both countries. The United States will continue to stand with the Sudanese and South Sudanese people and will work to ensure that this resolution is implemented in full.
